1.pericope_label: The strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please themselves

schools.summary: Calvin asks what the strength was given for. Lest those who had advanced further should think it unreasonable that more burden was laid on them, Paul shows why they excelled: as God destines those to whom he grants superior knowledge to instruct the ignorant, so to those whom he makes strong he commits the duty of supporting the weak, all gifts being thus communicated among the members of Christ. The stronger a man is in Christ, the more bound to bear with the weak. Calvin presses the verb further than tolerance will reach: the word rendered strong means able, and those called weak the unable, such as cannot carry their own burdens; the duty is not merely to bear with weaknesses, which is not the meaning of the verb, but to help the feeble to carry them, the most literal rendering being that we who are able ought to carry the infirmities of the unable. On the second clause he observes that nothing checks acts of kindness more than when a man is too much swallowed up with himself. Gill will not confine the term to ministers of the gospel — men of strong parts, mighty in the Scriptures, valiant for the truth, pillars in God's house — for though the apostle includes himself he writes not merely as such; the stronger part of private Christians are meant, the Apostle John's young men, strong as distinguished from newborn babes on the one hand and fathers on the decline of life on the other.

Henry begins from the common case. We all have our infirmities, but the weak are more subject to them — the weak in knowledge or grace, the bruised reed and the smoking flax; these we must consider, not trample upon but encourage. If through weakness they judge and censure us, we must bear with them and pity them, and not have our affections alienated; alas, it is their weakness, they cannot help it, and thus Christ bore with his weak disciples and apologised for them. But there is more in it than endurance, for we must bear their infirmities by sympathising with them, concerning ourselves for them, ministering strength as occasion serves, which is bearing one another's burdens.

Wesley defines the strong as of a clearer judgment, free from these scruples, and pleasing ourselves as acting without regard to others. Clarke states the obligation at its strongest: those who perfectly understand gospel liberty not only lawfully may but are bound in duty to bear any inconvenience arising from the scruples of weaker brethren, easing their consciences by prudently abstaining from indifferent things that may offend, and not using their superior knowledge to make the weak submit to their judgment.

Robertson notes that Paul identifies himself with one wing of the controversy, and that the strong here are the morally strong, not the mighty of the first epistle to Corinth. Barnes traces the word for bearing: it properly means to lift up, to bear away, to remove, but is used here in a larger sense, to bear with, to be indulgent, to endure patiently. Ellicott reads the duty out of the connection: the opening verses are intimately bound to the close of the previous chapter, since not only ought the strong to be careful in the matter of meat and drink, but in all things to show sympathy for their weaker brethren; and this unbroken continuity is enough of itself to show that the epistle cannot originally have ended where the fourteenth chapter ends. To bear the infirmities is to take them upon ourselves, act as if they were our own, and by our sympathy relieve the consciences of the weak.

themes: we then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak
and not to please ourselves
who the strong are

2.pericope_label: Please his neighbour for his good to edification, for even Christ pleased not himself

schools.summary: Calvin finds two things laid down: that we are not to be content with our own judgment nor acquiesce in our own desires, but to strive and labour at all times to please our brethren; and that in accommodating ourselves to them we must have regard to God, so that our object may be their edification. He then turns the qualification into a warning. The greater part cannot be pleased unless you indulge their humour, so that if you wish to be in favour with most, their salvation must not be much regarded but their folly flattered, and you must look not to what is expedient but to what they seek to their ruin. You must not then strive to please those to whom nothing is pleasing but evil. On the example itself Calvin argues from the servant's place: since it is not right that a servant refuse what his lord has undertaken, it would be strange in us to wish exemption from bearing the infirmities of others, to which Christ, in whom we glory as Lord and King, submitted himself. And he lets the quoted psalm cut both ways: away with those whose highest wish is to gain honours from men who treat God's name with all kinds of reproaches and persecute his gospel with sword and flame. Gill takes the pleasing to be a matter of manner as much as substance: a man should please his neighbour in all things lawful, carrying it affably and courteously, accommodating himself to his neighbour's weakness, and denying himself rather than displease him. He adds that Christ came not to be ministered to, as an earthly prince enjoying his ease, but to minister, in the form of a servant; yet not but that he was well pleased in it all, for it was his meat and drink to finish his work.

Clarke makes it a maxim that we do all in our power to please our brethren, especially where their edification is concerned; and though we should not indulge men in mere whims and caprices, we should bear with their ignorance and weakness, knowing that others had much to bear from us before we came to our present state of religious knowledge. Wesley notes that Christ bore not the infirmities only but the reproaches of his brethren.

Barnes narrows the word neighbour, which refers here especially to members of the church, though often used more largely; and for his good means not indulgence in things injurious, but whatever would promote his welfare. On the example he guards against a misreading: that Christ pleased not himself is not to be understood as if he did not voluntarily and cheerfully engage in his great work, for he was not compelled to come and suffer, nor as if he did not see its fitness, since otherwise he had never engaged in its self-denials. What is meant is that he came to do the will of God, not consulting his own happiness and honour in heaven; that he endured whatever trials that will might demand; that he sought neither comfort nor wealth nor honours, being poor that others might be rich; and that he bore with patience the ignorance and the ambitious projects of his disciples. Robertson puts the limit in a phrase: not to please men for popular favours, but for their benefit. Ellicott adds that the object of this tender dealing is their growth in spiritual perfection, grounded on the example of Christ himself.

themes: let every one of us please his neighbour for his good to edification
for even Christ pleased not himself
the reproaches of them that reproached thee fell on me

4.pericope_label: Whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning

schools.summary: Gill treats the verse as a vindication of the citation just made. What was written in that psalm did not belong personally to David but to Christ, and what is written concerning him is designed for the instruction of his people. Calvin takes it as a statement about the whole of Scripture. There is nothing vain or unprofitable in the oracles of God, and it is by reading Scripture that we make progress in piety and holiness of life; whatever is delivered there we ought to strive to learn, for it were a reproach to the Holy Spirit to think he has taught anything which it does not concern us to know. Though Paul speaks of the Old Testament, the same is true of the apostles' writings, since the Spirit of Christ is everywhere like itself. He finds here a most striking condemnation of those fanatics who vaunt that the Old Testament is abolished and belongs not in any degree to Christians — with what front, he asks, can they turn Christians from things which, as Paul testifies, God appointed for their salvation? He adds a definition of the patience meant: not that hardihood which the philosophers recommend, but that meekness by which we willingly submit to God, while a taste of his goodness and paternal love renders all things sweet.

Clarke reads the same universality out of it. God had not intended these writings merely for the generations to which they were first delivered, but for all succeeding generations; and it is through those remarkable examples of patience exhibited by the saints whose history is given there, and the comfort they derived from God in enduring sufferings brought on them by their attachment to truth, that we may hope to be upheld as they were. Wesley states the sequence plainly: through the consolation God gives by these we may have patience, and a joyful hope.

Barnes reads it as an aside. The apostle had just used a striking passage from the Psalms, and the thought seems suddenly to have occurred to him that the whole Old Testament was admirably adapted to express Christian duty and doctrine; the verse should be read as a parenthesis. He is careful with the next clause: through patience does not mean, as the English might suggest, the patience of the Scriptures, but that by patiently enduring sufferings, with the consolation the Scriptures furnish, we might have hope. Three lessons follow: that afflictions may prove a great blessing, that their tendency is to produce hope, and that the way to find support in affliction is to go to the Bible, learning from the recorded confidence of the ancient saints both how to suffer and where to find comfort. Robertson notes the present subjunctive of the last verb: that we might keep on having hope, one of the blessed uses of the Scriptures. Ellicott presses the article: it is literally the hope, the Messianic hope, since the promises of Scripture centre in the future glory, and the fortitude with which the Christian endures is sustained by that hope and reacts upon it, making it held with firmer tenacity.

debates.question: Does the word rendered comfort mean consolation or exhortation?

positions.position: it means also exhortation or admonition, and which sense is meant here is not easy to determine
some would render it exhortation, but there is no need to leave the usual acceptation, since comfort makes a consistent sense
exhortation is not to be disapproved, but consolation is the more suitable to patience, since patience arises from it

themes: whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning
through patience and comfort of the scriptures
that we might have hope

5.pericope_label: The God of patience grant you to be likeminded, that with one mind and one mouth ye may glorify God

schools.summary: Gill observes that the titles are chosen from what was just said about the Scriptures, to show that their efficacy in producing patience and comfort depends entirely on God their author; and that from exhorting the apostle proceeds to petitioning, knowing his exhortations would be of no avail without divine grace. The heathen so felt patience to be a divine blessing that they called it the invention of the gods. He draws the consequence for worship: a cordial and sincere affection for one another is necessary to worshipping God with one consent, for how should there be an agreement of heart and voice, of mind and mouth, unless there is a singleness of heart? Calvin adds why the prayer follows the exhortation: having admonished the Romans what they were to do, Paul turns to pray for them, understanding that to speak of duty was to no purpose except God inwardly effected by his Spirit what was spoken by the mouth of man. He makes God's glory depend on the unity asked for: God is not truly glorified unless the hearts of all agree in giving him praise and their tongues join in harmony; no one may boast that he will glorify God after his own manner, for the unity of his servants is so esteemed that God will not have his glory sounded forth amidst discords — a thought which ought to check the wanton rage for contention that at this day too much possesses the minds of many.

Henry makes it a rule for the ministry: faithful ministers water their preaching with their prayers, because whoever sows the seed it is God that gives the increase; we can but speak to the ear, it being God's prerogative to speak to the heart. Patience and comfort come through the Scripture as the conduit-pipe but from God as the fountain-head, and the more we receive of them the better disposed we are to love one another, since nothing breaks the peace more than an impatient, peevish and fretful temper. He lays the foundation of Christian love in like-mindedness, a consent in judgment as far as men have attained, or at least a concord in affection — but not at any price. Christ must be the centre of the unity: agree in the truth, not in any error. It was a cursed concord of those of one mind to give their power and strength to the beast, a like-mindedness not according to Christ but against him, like the Babel-builders who were one in their rebellion. The method of our prayer must therefore be first for truth and then for peace, for such is the wisdom from above, first pure and then peaceable.

Clarke reads the prayer as aimed at the assemblies themselves, since the dissensions between converted Jews and Gentiles might have greatly interrupted public worship; having done all that was needful by instruction and exhortation, the apostle pours out his soul to God, who alone could rule the heart, that all might join in the sweetest harmony in every act of worship. Wesley reads the one mind and one mouth as Jews and Gentiles together, believing with the one, confessing with the other.

Barnes takes the example for the argument: God bears long with his children and is not soon angry at their offences, a strong reason why Christians should bear with each other. He puts the negative case for worship: divisions and contention in the church prevent union in worship, so that though the church be professedly engaged in it, the service is divided, and the prayers of strife are not heard. Ellicott meets the objection that the verse's two halves hardly belong together. There seems at first sight little connection between the God of patience and the being likeminded; they are joined through the idea of singleness of aim, since he who is wholly self-dedicated to Christ, and in that strength endures persecution, will have a close bond with all who set the same object before them. Robertson notes that the word for one accord stands here alone in Paul though eleven times in Acts, a vivid outward expression of unity of feeling.

themes: now the God of patience and consolation grant you to be likeminded
according to Christ Jesus
that ye may with one mind and one mouth glorify God

7.pericope_label: Receive ye one another, as Christ also received us, to the glory of God

schools.summary: Gill reads the receiving as an act of the affections: embrace one another cordially, Jew the Gentile and Gentile the Jew, the strong brother the weak and the weak the strong. Calvin will not have the closing words parenthetic, and applies them to Christ and to us together: as Christ made known the glory of the Father in receiving us into favour when we stood in need of mercy, so it behoves us, to make known the glory of the same God, to establish and confirm this union which we have in Christ. He presses the plural: Christ took not one or two of us but all together, and has thus connected us, so that we ought to cherish one another if we would continue in his bosom; only thus shall we confirm our calling, if we separate not ourselves from those whom the Lord has bound together.

Henry notices that the shyness runs both ways: the prejudices of the weak make him shy of the strong as much as the pride of the strong makes him shy of the weak, and neither ought to be; let there be a mutual embracing among Christians. Those who have received Christ by faith must receive all Christians by brotherly love: though poor in the world, though persecuted and despised, though it may be matter of reproach and danger to receive them, though in the less weighty matters of the law of different apprehensions, though there may have been occasion for private piques; laying all such aside, receive one another. The reason is taken from the condescending love of Christ; can there be a more cogent argument? Has Christ been so kind to us, and shall we be so unkind to those that are his? He has received us into the nearest relations to himself — into his fold, his family, the adoption of sons, a covenant of friendship, yea a marriage-covenant — and that though we were strangers and enemies and had played the prodigal. Henry closes with a maxim of the schools, that things which agree with a third thing agree with each other: those who agree in Christ, the great centre of unity, may well afford to agree among themselves.

Clarke asks for the most affectionate regard, each acknowledging the other as the servants and children of God Almighty, with the same cordial affection with which Christ admitted us into communion with himself; so should Jews and Gentiles receive each other, that God's glory may be promoted by their harmony.

Ellicott reports a division in the manuscripts: the Vatican and Claromontane read received us, the Sinaitic, Alexandrine, Paris rescript and others received you; the latter is perhaps preferable, though with no real difference to the sense. The word received is the same as that at the beginning of the fourteenth chapter, whose subject is still continued and now taken up for the last time; and the duty of cordiality rests on the comprehensiveness of Christ's love, whose mission was directed with the same impartiality towards both. The closing words he takes for a parenthesis without direct bearing on the argument. Barnes gathers the argument into the word wherefore, which looks back over this chapter and the last: acknowledge one another as Christians and treat them as such, though you may differ about many smaller matters. Robertson notes that the repetition addresses both parties at once, strong and weak, and that the us takes in all.

themes: wherefore receive ye one another
as Christ also received us to the glory of God
the mutual embracing of strong and weak

8.pericope_label: Jesus Christ a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God

schools.summary: Chrysostom draws the debt the other way: the Gentiles are debtors to a larger amount, since the Jews had the good things by promise made to the fathers, while the Gentiles had them out of pity and love toward man only; and if the Gentiles owe the more, the more ought they to bear with the weak among the Jews.

Calvin sets the difference in its place. Christ embraced us all, and leaves no difference between Jew and Gentile except that he was first promised to the Jewish nation and in a manner peculiarly destined for them; but in the thing which was the seed of all their contentions there is no difference at all, for he gathered both out of a miserable dispersion and brought them into the Father's kingdom, that they might be one flock in one sheepfold under one shepherd. It is right therefore that they continue united and despise not one another, for Christ despised neither. Calvin then draws a consequence he thinks is missed. Since Christ came to fulfil what the Father had promised to Abraham, and that fulfilment must relate to eternal salvation, the old covenant was in reality spiritual though annexed to earthly types; and he marvels at the effrontery of those fanatical heads who regard the promises of the Old Testament as temporal and confine them to the present world. Either the benefits of Christ must be confined to temporal things, or the covenant made with Abraham must be extended beyond the things of this world. Gill takes the verse as proof that Christ has received the Jews, who are therefore not to be despised though weak.

Henry finds two honours in the phrase. That Christ was a minister at all bespeaks his exemplary condescension and puts an honour upon the ministry; but that he was a minister of the circumcision, being himself circumcised and made under the law and preaching the gospel in his own person to the Jews, makes that nation more considerable than it otherwise appears. He conversed with them and blessed them, looking on himself as primarily sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.

Wesley pauses on the order of the words. Jesus is the name and Christ the surname; the latter first known to the Jews, the former to the Gentiles, so that he is styled Jesus Christ when the words stand in their natural order, but when the order is inverted, as here, the office is the more solemnly considered. Clarke turns the verse against Gentile contempt. To show the Gentiles the propriety of bearing with the scrupulous Jews he reminds them of their obligations to that people, to whom in the days of his flesh Christ confined his ministry, allowing the Jews the first right to the blessings of the gospel; and he confined it thus to confirm the truth of God contained in the promises made to the patriarchs, so that salvation is of the Jews, a kind of right conveyed through those promises — though never designed exclusively for them.

Barnes presses the point on the translators: the force of the apostle's reasoning would often be more striking if the word Messiah were retained instead of treating Christ as a mere surname, since it is the name of an office, and to a Jew conveyed far more than a proper name. Robertson notes that the genitive is objective, a minister to the circumcision, and that no word answers to given in the Greek, which has simply the promises to the fathers. Ellicott would render the opening not now but for, and states the doctrine as a double mission: to the Jews, the chosen circumcised race, to vindicate the truthfulness of God in his promises by himself confirming and fulfilling them; and to the Gentiles, to exhibit the mercy of God in rescuing them from condemnation.

themes: Jesus Christ was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God
to confirm the promises made unto the fathers
what the Jews are owed

9.pericope_label: That the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy

schools.summary: Gill marks what the Gentiles owe thanks for. What they enjoy is not held by promise, as the Jews held theirs, but of mere mercy; not that promises do not arise from grace, though their accomplishment is owing to faithfulness, but that no promise was ever made to the Gentiles and yet they obtained mercy — while many were made concerning them, predictions in their favour standing on the divine record, some of which the apostle now produces. Calvin says the apostle dwells longer on this second point because it was less evident, and finds in the psalm, recorded also in the second book of Samuel, a prophecy of the kingdom of Christ from which the calling of the nations may be proved: it is there promised that a confession to God's glory should be made among them, and we cannot really make God known except among those who hear his praises while they are sung by us. Hence, that his name may be known among them, they must themselves be favoured with the knowledge of him and come into communion with his people; for this may be observed everywhere in Scripture, that God's praises cannot be declared except in the assembly of the faithful, who have ears capable of hearing them.

Clarke draws the division sharply: as the Jews were to glorify God for his truth, so the Gentiles for his mercy. The Jews received the blessings of the gospel by right of promise, which God had most punctually fulfilled; the Gentiles received the same gospel as an effect of mere mercy, having no right from any promise made with their ancestors, though the prophets had repeatedly declared they should be equal partakers. He then produces a maxim from the tract Megillah which concedes the point: from the time the children of Israel entered the promised land, no Gentile had any right to sing a hymn of praise to God; but after Israel was led into captivity, then the Gentiles began to have that right. Thus the Jews themselves confess it, and this on account of being made partakers of his grace. And with Schoettgen he presses it further: if they have a right to glorify God, their worship must be pleasing to him, and if pleasing then good, since otherwise God could not be pleased with it. Wesley notes that in the eighteenth psalm Gentiles and Jews are spoken of as joining in the worship of the God of Israel.

Ellicott states the contrast as a difference in the attribute displayed. The Jews had their covenant to appeal to, and what Christianity brought home to them most clearly was God's veracity in fulfilling the promises it contained; the Gentiles had no such covenant, and their admission was an act of pure grace, which they could only thankfully recognise. On the quotation he takes the eighteenth psalm to be David's own, a review of his past life and a thanksgiving for deliverance, in which David stands as a type of Christ, who is said to confess to God among the nations inasmuch as he is head of the Gentile church, in whose name its praises are offered. Barnes is careful about the fit between the psalm and the use made of it. The words are David's, who says he will praise God among the heathen, or when surrounded by them, acknowledging God's mercies as we should say to all the world; the apostle uses them to say the Gentiles would join with the Jew in offering praise, and Barnes grants plainly that this does not appear to have been David's original design, though the words express the idea of the apostle. Robertson observes that the position is proved by a chain of Old Testament quotations, and that the Gentiles were called through the promise to the Jews in the covenant with Abraham: salvation is of the Jews.

themes: that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy
I will confess to thee among the Gentiles, and sing unto thy name
truth to the Jews, mercy to the Gentiles

10.pericope_label: The catena of Gentile scriptures: rejoice, praise, and the root of Jesse

schools.summary: Calvin will not have the first verse from Moses at all. Moses' design there, he argues, was to terrify the adversaries of Israel by setting forth God's greatness, not to invite them to a common joy; he therefore takes the words from the forty-seventh psalm, where the prophet connects the Gentiles with Israel and invites both alike to rejoice. And there is no joy, he adds, without the knowledge of God. On the second he turns to an argument from the nature of praise: how can they praise him who know not his greatness? They could no more do that than call upon a name unknown to them. It is therefore a prophecy most suitable to prove their calling, the more so from the reason the psalm adds, bidding them give thanks for God's truth and mercy. The third Calvin calls the most illustrious of all. The prophet, when things were almost past hope, comforted the small remnant of the faithful with this, that a shoot would arise from the dry and dying trunk of David's family, and a branch flourish from his despised root to restore God's people their pristine glory; and it is clear from the account there given that this shoot was Christ, the Redeemer of the world. Twice over in that one prophecy he finds their calling confirmed — in the raising up of Christ as a sign, and in the declaration that they shall hope in him, which cannot take place without the preaching of the word and the illumination of the Spirit; and hope in Christ, he adds, is an evidence of his divinity.
Wesley observes that kings and the Messiah should spring from Jesse's house was promised to him before ever it was to David, and that those who now hope had before been without hope.

Barnes takes the first citation from the song of Moses, where the nations are called to rejoice with the Jews for God's interposition on their behalf; the design, he says, is to show that the Old Testament itself calls the Gentiles to celebrate God's praises, from which it follows that they come to the same privileges as his people. On the second he explains the method rather than the matter: the apostle accumulates quotations to show this was the common language of the Old Testament, and that he did not depend on a single expression for his doctrine; the psalm is directly in point, a call on all nations to praise God. On the third he works the figure out botanically: when a tree dies and falls, the root may yet retain life and send up a sprout of the same kind, as Job says there is hope of a tree if it be cut down; so though Jesse fell like an aged tree, his name and family were not extinct, and Jesus rose from a family fallen into poverty by the time of Mary. Ellicott grants that Paul follows the Septuagint, which here varies from the original, and reports the Hebrew sense disputed: the rendering which best suits the context, rejoice O ye nations of his people, meaning the Jewish tribes, is questioned on linguistic grounds, and the Vulgate reads instead, ye nations, praise his people. He hears an invitation addressed to the Gentile peoples without restriction, at a time when the conception of God as Lord of the whole earth was thoroughly established; and he would render the last citation strictly the root-shoot of Jesse, the expected descendant of that line, identified with the root itself to bring out its connection with the founder and distinguish it from collateral branches. He notices that the word rendered trust is the same as hope in the next verse, whose introduction was probably suggested by association from the closing words of this quotation. Robertson makes the word mean not the root but the sprout from it.

debates.question: Where is the second citation taken from?

positions.position: from the song of Moses in Deuteronomy, given as the Septuagint has it
not from Moses at all, whose design there was to terrify Israel’s adversaries rather than invite them to a common joy, but from the forty-seventh psalm

themes: rejoice, ye Gentiles, with his people
praise the Lord, all ye Gentiles
there shall be a root of Jesse, and in him shall the Gentiles trust

13.pericope_label: Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing

schools.summary: Gill derives the title from the words just quoted, in whom the Gentiles shall hope. God is the author and giver of that grace, for naturally men are without it, and a good hope is his gift, wrought in the heart in regeneration; he is also its object, since it terminates not on wealth and riches nor on works of righteousness but on God himself. Calvin asks why the passage should close with a prayer at all, and answers that the apostle desires the Lord to give whatever he had commanded. It hence appears that the Lord does not measure his precepts by our strength or the power of free will, nor command what we ought to do so that we, relying on our own power, may gird up ourselves to obey; rather he commands what requires the aid of his grace, that he may stimulate us to prayer. He would have faith connected with both the peace and the joy, being the bond of holy and legitimate concord and the support of godly joy; and that our peace may be approved by God we must be bound together by real and genuine faith.

Henry makes the address itself a lesson in prayer. It is good in prayer to fasten upon those names and attributes of God most suitable to the errand we come upon; every word in the prayer should be a plea, and thus should the cause be skilfully ordered and the mouth filled with arguments. God is both the object of our hope and the author of it; and that hope is but fancy, and will deceive us, which is not fastened upon God and not of his working in us. On the joy asked for, Henry sets the true against the counterfeit: carnal joy puffs up the soul but cannot fill it, and therefore even in laughter the heart is sad, whereas true spiritual joy is filling, having a satisfaction answerable to the soul's vast and just desires. He presses the word all. When we come to God by prayer we must enlarge our desires, for we are not straitened in him, and why then should we be straitened in ourselves? Ask for all joy; open thy mouth wide, and he will fill it. And since the joy and peace of believers arise chiefly from their hopes, and what is laid out upon them is but little compared with what is laid up for them, the more hope they have the more joy and peace they have.

Wesley calls the title glorious, and till then unknown to the heathens, whose goddess Hope, like their other idols, was nothing — her temple at Rome was burned by lightning, and though it was built again not long after, it was again burned to the ground. Clarke reads it as the God of this hope in particular, who caused both Jews and Gentiles to hope that the promises made them should be fulfilled, and has fulfilled them punctually; the joy asked for them is true spiritual happiness, peace in their own hearts and unity among themselves.

Ellicott takes the three words as a triad representing the Christian's attitude toward the future, and so far as that future is reflected on the present; hope may be taken as including the other two, since it is on the certainty of the Messianic promises that all three depend, and through the energising of the Holy Spirit that they are kept alive. Barnes states the consequence in a line: if they were filled with this, there would be no strife and contention among them, for the effect of believing is to produce such joy and peace. Robertson notes that the verb is again an optative of wish for the future, that the phrase is literally in the believing, and that the verse gathers up the points of all the preceding quotations.

themes: now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing
that ye may abound in hope
through the power of the Holy Ghost

14.pericope_label: I myself am persuaded of you, that ye are full of goodness and able to admonish one another

schools.summary: Chrysostom hears a softening. Having often made his language harsh, the apostle now speaks kindly; and he does not say I have heard but I am persuaded, as needing no report from others, nor ye have goodness but ye are full of it — as if to say, it was not because you were cruel, or haters of your brethren, that I so exhorted you.

Gill takes the sentence as forestalling an objection: what does the apostle take us for, that he prays and exhorts at such length — men devoid of humanity, a parcel of ignorant men, with none fit to give an admonition? He answers that, never having seen them, he yet had such an account of their faith and practice as persuaded him of better things. Calvin sets out what qualifies a man to admonish at all. Two things are especially necessary: kindness, which disposes the mind to aid one's brethren by advice and tempers the countenance and the words with courtesy; and skill in advice, or prudence, which secures authority to him, inasmuch as he is able to benefit those he addresses. Nothing is more opposed to brotherly admonition than malignity and arrogance, which make us disdainfully despise the erring and treat them with ridicule rather than set them right; and asperity, whether it appears in the words or in the countenance, deprives our admonitions of their fruit. Calvin adds what the apostle was up against. There was much pride in the Romans, the very name of their city making the lowest of the people proud, so that they could hardly bear a teacher of another nation, much less a barbarian and a Jew.

Henry insists the praise was earned: not idle flattery and compliment, but a due acknowledgment of their worth and of the grace of God in them; and it was a great credit to be commended by Paul, a man too skilful to be deceived and too honest to flatter. On their being able to admonish one another he adds a wish and a warning together: it is a comfort to faithful ministers to see their work superseded by the gifts and graces of their people, and would to God that all the Lord's people were prophets — but that which is everybody's work is nobody's work.

Wesley notes that this verse begins the first of the epistle's several conclusions, and glosses the commendations: full of goodness by being created anew, filled with all knowledge by long experience of the things of God. Clarke reports two variants: some manuscripts of good repute read love for goodness, which here comes to nearly the same thing; and several read others rather than one another, which he thinks the clearer sense, since if all were filled with knowledge there was little occasion to admonish each other, though they were well qualified to admonish those less instructed.

Ellicott marks the turn of the letter. From this point the apostle gives it a personal cast; the more necessary because the church at Rome was not one of his own founding, so that he might seem to be going out of his way, and even acting against his own principles, in writing to them at all. Robertson agrees the epilogue begins here, the argument being complete, and warns that the all knowledge is not to be pressed literally. Barnes draws a rule for ministers out of the apostle's manner. There is no impropriety in commending Christians when they deserve it, and Paul, when reproof was needed, gave it with tenderness and tears, but where he could commend he preferred to; whereas the minister who always censures and condemns, whose ministry is made up of complaints and lamentations, and who never speaks of Christians but in a strain of fault-finding, is unlike the example of the Saviour and of Paul, and may expect little success in his work.

themes: I myself also am persuaded of you, my brethren
that ye also are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge
able also to admonish one another

15.pericope_label: The grace given me, that I should be the minister of Jesus Christ to the Gentiles

schools.summary: Gill takes the boldness to lie in his noticing their party contentions and ill usage of each other, and in reproving them at all. Calvin sees the modesty and the claim held together. Paul concedes that he acted boldly in interposing in a matter they could themselves manage, but was led to it by his office; and he so humbles himself as to exalt that office, for by mentioning the favour of God which raised him to it he shows that what he did as an apostle could not be despised. He denies, too, that he had assumed the part of a teacher, but only that of an admonisher. On the priestly language Gill sets the office against two that might be confused with it: Paul was no minister in holy things about the temple, as the priests and Levites were, nor a teacher of the law, but a minister of Christ and a preacher of him, since Christ crucified was the grand subject of his ministrations.

Wesley states the ground shortly: because I am an apostle of the Gentiles. Clarke, with Whitby, finds a plain allusion to the Jewish sacrifices, made acceptable by the libation offered with them: in preaching the gospel the apostle compares himself to the priest preparing his sacrifice; the Gentiles converted by him and dedicated to God are his sacrifice and oblation, and the Holy Spirit is the libation poured upon it, by which it is sanctified and rendered acceptable.

Barnes reports that some referred the qualifying phrase to a party at Rome, others to particular passages of the epistle, but thinks it probably qualifies the boldness itself, the phrase, as Grotius says, diminishing that of which it is spoken. He weighs the priestly words carefully, and will not let them prove too much. The word rendered minister is not the common one but a term used of those who serve in public offices, applied in the New Testament chiefly to the Levitical priesthood; and the word rendered ministering means performing a priest's office, whose business was to offer sacrifice. The Jewish sacrifices were abolished, the Messiah having fulfilled the design of their appointment, and there was to be no further literal sacrifice. Paul retains the language without implying that the ministers of the New Testament are literally priests, and did not mean that the Gentiles' offerings were literal sacrifices to expiate sins, nor that there was to be an order of men called priests under the new covenant — and if the passage proved that, Barnes observes, it would prove the order confined to the apostles, since it is of them only that Paul uses it. He notes too how a sacrifice was made fit among the Jews, by salt, oil or frankincense; the Gentiles' offering was rendered holy not by these but by the cleansing influences of God's Spirit. Robertson finds the reference in those places where the apostle has spoken plainly, and notes that the verb for putting in mind is a rare compound found nowhere else in the New Testament, meaning as if calling back to mind. Ellicott hears the sentence as an apology: holding this good opinion of them, the apostle nevertheless presumed on his position to write with an earnestness he might otherwise not have ventured; in some passages he feels he had gone beyond the limits he had marked out for himself, taking a liberty, though not too great a liberty. He distinguishes the two Greek words as allied but not identical, the first covering the whole liturgical service of priests and Levites, the second the priests' special function in sacrifice; and he insists on the genitive, that the offering up of the Gentiles means not what the Gentiles offer but the offering which the Gentiles are, the sacrifice they themselves constitute. The last clause he would render not sanctified by but consecrated in the Holy Ghost.

themes: I have written the more boldly unto you in some sort
because of the grace that is given to me of God
ministering the gospel of God, that the offering up of the Gentiles might be acceptable

17.pericope_label: I have therefore whereof I may glory through Jesus Christ in those things which pertain to God

schools.summary: Gill lists what the apostle is not glorying in. He who taught others not to glory in men would not glory in himself: not in his carnal descent and fleshly privileges, nor in his compliance with the ceremonies of the law, nor in his legal and civil righteousness, nor in his gifts as though merited by himself, nor in his labours as of himself. Calvin explains why the passage is there at all. Having commended his calling in general, that the Romans might know him for a true apostle of Christ, Paul adds testimonies proving that he had not only taken the apostolic office by God's appointment but had eminently adorned it, and records the fidelity he showed in discharging it; for it is to little purpose that we are appointed, except we act agreeably to our calling. He made the declaration from no desire of glory, but because nothing was to be omitted which might procure favour and authority for his doctrine; he gloried in God, not in himself. That he speaks at first only negatively Calvin takes for evidence of his modesty, which yet served to gain credit for what he was about to announce — as though he had said, the truth itself affords me such cause for glorying that I need seek no false praises, nor another man's; I am content with such as are true.

Henry asks what the Romans were to get from another man's travels, and answers that it was for their encouragement: they were not alone in the profession of Christianity, but, though a little flock beside the multitude of their idolatrous neighbours, up and down the country there were many who were their companions in the kingdom and patience of Jesus Christ. The glorying itself Henry describes as not vain glory but holy gracious glorying, as appears from the limitations set on it, that it is through Jesus Christ and in those things which pertain to God — for the conversion of souls pertains to God, and may therefore be matter of glorying, as the things of the flesh may not. On the claim to have fully preached the gospel Henry lingers over the word, which is properly filled: he filled the gospel as a net is filled with fishes in a large draught, or filled them with the gospel; and such a change does the gospel make that when it comes in power to any place it fills the place, for other knowledge is airy and leaves souls empty, but the knowledge of the gospel is filling. He notices too the protestation that follows, that Paul dared not speak of anything Christ had not wrought by him: he would not boast beyond his line, nor take the praise of another man's work, as he might easily have done writing to distant strangers who could not contradict him — a faithful man dares not lie, however he be tempted, and dares be true, however he be terrified.

Wesley puts the positive shortly: all his glorying is in and through Christ. Clarke allows a double ground of exultation, he being sent of God on so honourable an errand: the honour conferred on him, and the success with which God crowned his ministry.

Barnes draws from the word the rule for every minister after him: a minister's success is not for his own praises but for the honour of God, and comes not by his skill but by the aid of Christ, yet he may rejoice that through him such blessings are conferred on men. Ellicott takes the verse for the title on which the apostle rests his claim, a sacred office given him by Christ and not of his own devising, whose sphere is a religious one; Robertson renders the last phrase as to the things relating to God.

themes: I have therefore whereof I may glory through Jesus Christ
in those things which pertain to God
the difference between vain glory and holy glorying

18.pericope_label: From Jerusalem round about unto Illyricum I have fully preached the gospel of Christ

schools.summary: Gill hears the disclaimer aimed at rivals: the false teachers spoke of things not done by them at all, much less by Christ through them, whereas the apostle could speak nothing but truth, his conscience not suffering him to mention anything as done by himself rather than wrought by Christ. He grants the signs their force and their limit: they carried evidence and conviction of what was delivered, and wrought powerfully on the minds of the Gentiles to embrace the gospel, though all would have been insufficient without the power of the Spirit named next. Calvin explains what the recital is for. These words prove that his object was to render his ministry approved by the Romans, that his doctrine might not be without fruit; and he proves by evidences that God, by the presence of his power, had given testimony to his preaching and in a manner sealed his apostleship, so that none ought to have doubted that he was appointed and sent by the Lord. Calvin then states what miracles are for: they were testimonies of divine power to awaken men, that being struck with God's power they might admire and adore him, and so are designed to prepare men to reverence and obey God. From which he draws a test with an edge on it: those miracles which bring glory to creatures and not to God, and which secure credit to lies and not to God's word, are from the devil.

Clarke takes the pair of words for the doctrines the apostle taught and the miracles he wrought, so that the Gentiles became obedient to the doctrines on the evidence of the miracles that accompanied them. He collects the names the country has borne among ancient writers — Illyria, Illyrica, Illyris, Illyrium — and notes that it now forms part of Croatia, Bosnia, Istria and Slavonia.

Barnes states the restraint plainly: he confines himself to what he has done, does not arrogate what Christ has done by others, and does not exaggerate his own success. He explains why Jerusalem is named as the starting point: it was not where Paul began to preach, but where the gospel was first preached, and the apostles reckoned their success from that point; the round about means in a circle, taking Jerusalem as a centre. He notes that the Acts nowhere mentions Paul's going into Illyricum, nor does the expression imply that he preached within it, but only unto its borders; and he reckons up what the circle held — Damascus and Arabia, Syria, Asia Minor, all Greece, the Grecian islands, Thessaly and Macedonia, no small part of the then known world, all of it reached by the labours of one indefatigable man. Ellicott makes it a principle of the mission field: the apostle will take credit for no man's labours but his own, which have indeed been signal enough, since all successes there are due ultimately to Christ, who for some has used Paul and for others other men. He renders the phrase literally as through the might of signs and wonders, that is, through those extraordinary powers which found expression in them, the two words denoting the same acts but connoting different aspects. Robertson would render the disclaimer, any of those things Christ did not work through me, and reads the pair of words as by preaching and life.

debates.question: What does it mean that he fully preached the gospel?

positions.position: filled up, that is, diffused abroad, so that he had faithfully spread the knowledge of the gospel through all that immense country
successfully preached, since the word means not only fully but to teach with prosperity and success — he had made converts and founded churches

themes: I will not dare to speak of any of those things which Christ hath not wrought by me
through mighty signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God
from Jerusalem, and round about unto Illyricum

20.pericope_label: Striving to preach not where Christ was named, lest I should build on another man's foundation

schools.summary: Gill says the sense is not merely that the apostle strove to preach the gospel and not the law, nor only that he preached it fully, but that he had a holy ambition. Calvin turns the verse into a definition of the apostolic office as distinct from every later one. The work of an Apostle is to propagate the gospel where it has not been preached, according to the command, Go ye, preach the gospel to every creature; and this we ought to notice, lest we make a general rule of what belongs specially to the apostolic order, or count it a fault that a successor was substituted who built up the church. The apostles were as it were the founders of the church, and the pastors who succeeded them had to strengthen and amplify the building they raised. Calvin holds that Paul's apostleship was made evident from this circumstance, that the prophecy was fulfilled in him; and he closes with a warning against misapplying it. It is absurd to apply what is here said to the pastoral office, for in churches rightly formed, where the truth of the gospel has already been received, Christ's name must be constantly preached. Paul preached Christ to nations that knew him not for this very end, that after his departure the same doctrine should be daily proclaimed by the mouth of the pastors.

Clarke derives the word for striving from the words for a friend and for honour: I have considered it my honour to preach the gospel where it was before unknown. He adds what the choice cost: not watering what another had planted, but cheerfully exposing himself to dangers to found new churches. On the prophecy he is cautious: the apostle applies the words to his own conduct, not that they predicted what Paul had done, but that he endeavoured to fulfil such a declaration by his manner of preaching to the heathen. Wesley qualifies the rule twice. These places the apostle generally declined, though not altogether; and the providence of God seemed specially to prevent his building on another's foundation, though again not wholly, lest his enemies, who sought every occasion to set light by him, should have room to say that he was behind other apostles, not sufficient for planting churches but only for preaching where others had been already.

Barnes explains that the word means to be ambitious, to be studious of honour; and on the prophecy he notes that it is not literally quoted, though the sense is retained, the design being to justify the principle on which the apostle acted: it had been revealed that the gospel should be preached to the Gentiles, and he counted it a high honour to carry the prediction into effect. Ellicott would render it, making it my ambition, the apostle setting it before him as a point of honour not merely to carry on a work others had begun but to build the whole edifice from the foundation himself; and on the prophecy he looks back at the original, where the reference is to the servant of Jehovah, first suffering and then glorified, so that kings should be dumb with astonishment. Robertson calls it a noble word, quite unlike the Latin word for ambition, which means to go about on both sides to carry one's point; Paul, he says, was a pioneer preacher pushing into new fields after the manner of Daniel Boone in Kentucky, and though this ambition is beyond the range of some ministers, who can only build on another's foundation as Apollos did at Corinth, the pioneer preacher has a dignity and glory all his own. He reports that Fritzsche went the whole way, actually arguing that Paul understood Isaiah to be predicting his own ministry.

themes: so have I strived to preach the gospel, not where Christ was named
lest I should build upon another man’s foundation
to whom he was not spoken of, they shall see

22.pericope_label: For which cause also I have been much hindered from coming to you

schools.summary: Gill refers the hindrance to the years spent preaching from Jerusalem round about to Illyricum. Calvin reads the excuse as part of the commission: in propagating the gospel from Judea as far as Illyricum, Paul performed as it were a course enjoined by the Lord, which being accomplished he purposed not to neglect them; and lest they still think themselves neglected, he testifies that there had long been no want of desire. Calvin adds a caution about the plan that follows: from this passage is drawn a weak argument for his going into Spain, since it does not follow that he performed the journey because he intended it — he speaks only of a hope, in which he, like other faithful men, might sometimes have been frustrated.

Henry begins not with the matter but the manner. The subject is common and ordinary, a man appointing a visit to his friends, but the way of expressing it is gracious and savoury; we should learn by it to speak of our common affairs in the language of Canaan, for even our common discourse should have an air of grace, and by this it will appear what country we belong to. He observes that Paul's company was much desired at Rome, he being a man who had as many friends and as many enemies as most men ever had, and passed through evil report and good report. But Henry is careful about what Paul wanted to see. Not Rome, though then in its greatest pomp and splendour, nor the emperor's court, nor the philosophers and learned men then in the city, whose conversation must have been desirable to so great a scholar; but a company of poor despised saints, hated of the world but loving God and beloved of him, whose acquaintance he was the more ambitious of for the character they had in all the churches for faith and holiness. On the hindrance Henry draws out the providence. God's dearest servants are not always gratified in everything they have a mind to, though all who delight in God have the desire of their heart fulfilled. Paul was several times crossed in his intentions, hindered by Satan, forbidden by the Spirit, here diverted by other work; man purposes but God disposes, and the stars are in the right hand of Christ, to shine where he sets them, so the gospel comes to no place by chance but by the will and counsel of God. Henry adds what the delay proves of the man. Had Paul consulted his own ease, wealth and honour, the greatness of the work would never have hindered him from seeing Rome, but would rather have driven him thither, where he might have had more preferment and taken less pains; but he sought the things of Christ more than his own, and would not leave the planting of churches even for a time. The Romans were whole, and needed not the physician as those poor places that were sick and dying.

Clarke makes it turn on the principle just stated: considering it a point of honour to build on no other man's foundation, and finding the gospel planted at Rome long before, he was kept from going thither, purposing rather to spend his strength where Christ was not yet proclaimed. Wesley says the same: among whom Christ had been named.

Barnes insists the phrase means many ways rather than many times, the demands elsewhere being frequent and urgent; Ellicott takes it the other way, as these many times, so often. Robertson notes that the verb is an imperfect passive of a late word meaning to cut in, to cut off, to interrupt, so the hindrance was repeated, and it was Paul's own work that kept him away.

themes: for which cause also I have been much hindered from coming to you
the providence that overrules a minister’s purposes
why Rome was not the first call

23.pericope_label: Having no more place in these parts, I take my journey into Spain and will come by you

schools.summary: Gill says first what the want of room does not mean. It was not that persecution was too hot for him, which he expected everywhere and took pleasure in enduring for Christ's sake; it was that he had filled every town and city of those parts with the gospel, planted churches and ordained elders over them, so that no places were left but such as he or some other apostle had visited.

Clarke notes that the phrase means not merely a place of residence but convenience or opportunity, a frequent sense among the best Greek writers, and that the apostle was then at Corinth, having evangelised all those parts and having no opportunity of breaking up new ground. He is sharper still about what has been built on the region's Christian antiquity: legendary tales inform us that St James had planted the gospel there long before and founded many bishoprics, which is as unfounded as it is ridiculous and absurd, since nothing like what is now termed a bishopric, nor even a parish, was founded for many years after; an itinerant preacher, Clarke adds, might more properly say that travelling circuits were formed. He lingers over the word rendered filled, which he would rather render gratified, and supports the sense from the classics: Aelian uses it of the peacock spreading his plumage, who readily permits the spectator to gratify himself by viewing him. Wesley marvels at the modesty of it, since they might rather have desired to be satisfied with his company than he with theirs, and takes the somewhat to intimate the shortness of his stay — or perhaps that Christ alone can thoroughly satisfy the soul.

Ellicott takes place to mean room for new working, the whole ground being already occupied, and remarks that the word rendered parts is that from which our word climate is derived, its original idea being the slope of the earth from the equator towards the pole. Robertson calls the admission a surprising frankness that the average preacher would hardly use: Paul is now free to come to Rome because there is no demand for him where he is. Ellicott calls the qualification at the end a characteristic touch, since the apostle will not have it supposed that he could ever have enough of the society of the Roman church, and so says satisfied only in part; Robertson calls the phrase a delicate compliment. Barnes observes that even here the apostle does not say his principal object was to visit the church at Rome, but only to take it in his way in fulfilment of the higher purpose of preaching where Christ was not named.

positions.position: no — there is no evidence whatever that he went, the presumption is that he did not undertake the voyage, and antiquity affords no proof

perhaps rather more probable than not, on the tradition going back to Clement of Rome that he visited the extreme limit of the West, and the Muratorian Fragment; the argument from silence counts for little since the Acts stops short of his death

open — some fathers say he passed two years there after his release, and such a visit between two imprisonments is not improbable, but there is no certain evidence, and Paul probably projected many journeys never accomplished

themes: having no more place in these parts
whensoever I take my journey into Spain, I will come to you
if first I be somewhat filled with your company

25.pericope_label: Now I go unto Jerusalem to minister unto the saints, for Macedonia and Achaia have made a contribution

schools.summary: Chrysostom sees two things done at once. Having said that he had no more place in those parts and had long desired to come, the apostle still meant to delay; and lest it be thought that he was making a jest of them, he mentions the cause. But by this means he also makes good another object, the exhorting of them to alms. Had he not been minded to effect that, it had sufficed to say, I am going unto Jerusalem; instead he adds the reason of the journey, dwells on it, and enters into reasonings about debtors. There is much reason, Chrysostom says, to admire his wisdom in devising this way of giving the advice, for they were likelier to bear it so than in the form of exhortation, which would have seemed an insult had he set the Corinthians and Macedonians before them to incite them.

Calvin reads it the same way: though Paul does not openly ask the Romans for anything, by saying that Macedonia and Achaia had done what they ought he intimates that the Romans lay under the same obligation. He admires the givers: it was a rare instance of kindness that the Grecians, hearing that their brethren at Jerusalem laboured under want, considered not the distance that separated them, but, esteeming those sufficiently nigh to whom they were united by the bond of faith, relieved their necessities out of their own abundance. Gill notes that he was bound in spirit for Jerusalem, not knowing what should befall him there, nor could his friends dissuade him.

Clarke explains what the collection was for and what it was meant to do. The object of the journey was to carry a contribution made among the Gentile Christians of Macedonia and Achaia for the relief of the poor Jewish Christians at Jerusalem. He hoped that this liberal contribution, sent by Gentile converts, would engage the affections of the Jewish Christians, much prejudiced as they were against receiving the Gentiles into the church without their first submitting to the yoke of the law; he wished to establish a coalition between converted Jews and Gentiles, being sensible of its importance to the spread of the gospel, and this contribution was one laudable device to accomplish that end. Wesley presses the point further: it can by no means be inferred from the expression that the community of goods among the Christians had then ceased, since all that can be gathered is that in this time of extreme dearth some of the church in Jerusalem were in want, the rest being barely able to subsist themselves and not to supply their brethren.

Barnes observes that this intended journey is mentioned in several other places, and that Paley derived from the way it is mentioned a strong argument for the genuineness of the epistle; that he carried it out appears from his defence before Felix, that after many years he came to bring alms to his nation. Robertson notes that the verb rendered it hath pleased shows the giving was voluntary, that Paul does not mention Asia and Galatia, and that it is called a certain contribution because it was still unknown to the Romans; he calls the description of the recipients a partitive genitive. Ellicott renders it literally, for the poor among the saints, and infers that the church at Jerusalem cannot have consisted entirely of poor, though from the first men like Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus seem to have been exceptions, and the church there suffered severely during the famine under Claudius. He closes with the argument the apostle is about to use himself: from Jerusalem went forth the gospel preached in Greece and Macedonia, and it would be but a small and due return if some of the superfluous wealth of those more favoured regions found its way back.

themes: now I go unto Jerusalem to minister unto the saints
it hath pleased them of Macedonia and Achaia
to make a certain contribution for the poor saints which are at Jerusalem

27.pericope_label: Their debtors they are: if the Gentiles have been made partakers of their spiritual things

schools.summary: Gill dwells on the freedom of the gift: the first motion was from themselves, unasked, not by constraint but entirely free, and not for ostentation or to gain the applause of men, but from a principle of love to the poor saints; they gave not sparingly but largely, not grudgingly but cheerfully — and yet, Gill adds, did but what they ought. Calvin observes for whose sake the obligation is stated: not so much for the Corinthians as for the Romans themselves, for the Corinthians and Macedonians were no more indebted to the Jews than the Romans were; and the ground of it is that they had received the gospel from them. It shows the value of the gospel, Calvin adds, when the apostle declares them indebted not only to its ministers but to the whole nation from which those ministers came; and he does not doubt that Paul meant it for a kind of sacrifice when the faithful give of their own to relieve their brethren, since they thus perform the duty of love they owe and offer God a sacrifice of an acceptable odour. On the sealing Calvin does not disapprove of those who find here an allusion to the practice of the ancients, who closed with their seals whatever they meant to lay up in safety: Paul commends his own faithfulness, as though he had said that he was an honest keeper of money deposited with him, no otherwise than if he carried it sealed.

Wesley says they were bound to it in justice as well as mercy, and draws the lesson from the plan that follows, that there are often holy purposes in the minds of good men which the providence of God overrules so that they never take effect, and yet are precious in his sight. Clarke states what was owed and returned: it was through the Jews that the Gentiles had been brought to the knowledge of God, and these were the spiritual things they had received, the pecuniary contribution being the carnal things they now sent back; and on the plan he says only that Paul had fully purposed it, if God should see meet to permit him, but that it does not appear he ever went.

Robertson notes that the genitive is objective, the Gentiles being debtors to the Jews, and that the carnal things belong to the natural life of the flesh, with no reference to its sinful aspects; and he notes how keenly sensitive Paul was that this collection should be actually conveyed to Jerusalem free from all suspicion. Barnes turns the principle towards the maintenance of a ministry: on this ground the apostle elsewhere rests the obligation to support the ministers of the gospel, since it becomes a debt where the hearer receives, in spiritual blessings, far more than he confers by his support. The minister is not a beggar, and what is necessary to his support is not almsgiving; he has an equitable claim, as much as a physician or a lawyer or a teacher of youth. On the sealing Barnes explains that to seal a contract or deed is to authenticate it and make it sure, and that Paul meant to see for himself that the money was placed securely in their hands. Ellicott says the same in a sentence: they owed the church at Jerusalem a debt which it was their duty to discharge; and he grants that the expression will appear at first sight somewhat stilted, but thinks it takes a certain solemnity from the apostle's seeming to regard this journey to Jerusalem as the close of his own labours in those parts, the dropping of the curtain, as it were, before a new act in his career.

themes: their debtors they are
if the Gentiles have been made partakers of their spiritual things
when I have sealed to them this fruit, I will come by you into Spain

29.pericope_label: I shall come in the fulness of the blessing of the gospel of Christ

schools.summary: Gill marks the difference between the two halves of the plan. The apostle intended to go to Spain but was not sure of reaching it, whereas he was positive of arriving at Rome; that had been much and long upon his mind, and under an impress of the Spirit he had signified before this that after Jerusalem he must see Rome also, as it was afterwards told him expressly by the Lord that, as he had testified at Jerusalem, so he should bear witness at Rome. Calvin offers two ways of explaining the words. The first is that he should find a plentiful fruit already at Rome, since the blessing of the gospel is that it fructifies in good works — though to confine this to alms, as some do, Calvin does not approve. The second is that, to make his coming more an object of desire, he says he hopes it will not be unfruitful but will make a great accession to the gospel, which would depend partly on his ministry and partly on their faith. The former seems to Calvin the best: he hoped at his coming to find the gospel flourishing among them and prevailing with evident success, and themselves excelling in holiness and every other virtue, since the reason he gives for his desire is that he looked for no common joy in seeing them, expecting them to abound in all its spiritual riches.

Clarke reports that the words rendered of the gospel are wanting in almost every manuscript of importance and that Griesbach left them out; and he thinks the shorter reading says the more, since the fullness of the blessing of Christ is really more than the fullness of the blessing of the gospel of Christ — the apostle hoped to come endued with the gifts and graces of the Lord Jesus himself.

Barnes notes that the Greek is simply I know, expressing the fullest confidence, a confidence greatly strengthened by the success of his labours elsewhere; and that the phrase which follows is a Hebrew mode of expression, in which one noun does the work of an adjective and means with a full or abundant blessing. He reads the verse against what actually happened. Paul did go to Rome, but in bonds; and yet he was permitted to preach there for at least two years, nor can we doubt that his ministry had the success he anticipated. God may disappoint us in regard to the mode in which we purpose to do good, but if we really desire it he will enable us to do it in his own way; and it may be better to preach in bonds than at liberty, better even in a prison than not at all. Barnes finds a parallel nearer his own time. Bunyan wrote the Pilgrim's Progress to amuse his heavy hours during a twelve years' cruel imprisonment, and if he had been at liberty he probably would not have written it at all; the great desire of his heart was accomplished, but a prison was the place in which to do it. Paul preached, Barnes ends, but preached in chains. Ellicott agrees with the shorter reading, and takes the phrase for that full and abundant measure of spiritual treasures which Paul was commissioned to impart. Robertson observes that the participle is present with the force of the future, coming I shall come, and that the apostle had already told them at the opening of the epistle that he had a spiritual gift for Rome — a gift, Robertson adds, which he did bring.

themes: I am sure that, when I come unto you, I shall come in the fulness of the blessing
the shorter reading of the text
how the prayer was answered

30.pericope_label: Strive together with me in your prayers to God for me

schools.summary: Gill grounds the request on the relation named: as brethren they should love one another, and show it by praying for each other to their common parent. Calvin explains why the request is so urgent here. It is well known how much ill-will prevailed against Paul in his own nation on account of false reports, as though he taught a departure from Moses; and he knew how far calumnies might avail to oppress the innocent, especially among those carried away by inconsiderate zeal. The more peril he perceived, the more he was moved; nor let us wonder that he was anxious about a life in which he knew so much danger to the Church was involved. Yet he still went forward, not so dreading it but that he was prepared willingly to meet it, having recourse to the remedies God had given him. Calvin turns this on the reader. Since it is so great a favour to be helped by the prayers of the faithful that even Paul, a most choice instrument of God, did not neglect the privilege, how great must be our stupidity if we, abject and worthless creatures, disregard it? But to take a handle from such passages for maintaining the intercessions of dead saints is, he says, an instance of extreme effrontery. He ends by drawing out what the striving asks of us: the godly are to assume the person of those they pray for, as though placed in the same difficulties, for he who commends his brother to the Lord by taking to himself a part of his distress does so far relieve him; and if our own strength is derived from prayer, we can in no better way confirm our brethren than by praying for them.

Henry marks who it is that asks. Though a great apostle, Paul begged the prayers of the meanest Christians, not here only but in several other epistles; he had prayed much for them, and desires this as the return of his kindness, for interchanging prayers is an excellent token of the interchanging of loves. He takes the striving in two senses. We must strive in prayer, putting forth all that is within us, praying with fixedness, faith and fervency, wrestling with God as Jacob did, praying in praying as Elias did; and this not only for ourselves but for our friends, since true love to our brethren should make us as earnest for them as the sense of our own need makes us for ourselves. And we must strive together with him: when Paul begged their prayers he did not mean to excuse his own, but would have them ply the same oar. Those who are put far asunder by the disposal of God's providence may still meet together at the throne of his grace; and those who beg the prayers of others must not neglect to pray for themselves.

Clarke takes the second plea for that love of God which the Holy Spirit sheds abroad in the heart, and renders the verb simply, that ye agonize with me. Wesley says the same shortly, that he must pray himself who would have others strive together with him, and adds an observation about the apostle's habit: of all the apostles, Paul alone is recorded to desire the prayers of the faithful for himself, and he generally does it in the conclusions of his epistles.

Barnes explains the first plea as out of love and regard to Christ, to promote his honour among men; and on the word rendered strive he notes that it denotes the intense effort of wrestlers in the Greek games, and then the effort a man makes in prayer who is earnestly desirous to be heard. Ellicott takes the second plea for the love inspired in them by the Spirit. Robertson observes that the compound verb occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and points for Christ's own agony to Gethsemane.

themes: I beseech you, for the Lord Jesus Christ’s sake, and for the love of the Spirit
that ye strive together with me in your prayers to God for me
how the godly are to pray for their brethren

31.pericope_label: That I may be delivered from them that do not believe, and that my service may be accepted

schools.summary: Gill weighs who the unbelievers are. Some think men are meant who believed in Jesus yet were set against the apostle for preaching down the ceremonial law; rather, he judges, such as did not believe in Christ at all are designed, enemies to the gospel and to all its ministers, but especially to Paul for preaching among the Gentiles. He explains why both petitions had to be granted before the visit could be glad: unless delivered he could not come at all, and should the saints there use him ungratefully and slight the kindness of the Gentile churches, his coming would be with sorrow rather than joy. Calvin draws a lesson from the very doubt. Slanderers had so prevailed that the apostle feared the gift would hardly be acceptable from his hands, which otherwise, in such distress, would have been most seasonable; and hence his wonderful meekness, for he ceased not to labour for those of whom he doubted whether he would be welcome. This disposition we ought to imitate, that we may not cease to do good to those of whose gratitude we are by no means certain. Calvin notices too that he honours with the name of saints the very people by whom he feared he would be suspected; knowing that saints may be led away by false slanders into unfavourable opinions, and that these wronged him, he yet spoke honourably of them. He makes the same point from the Romans' side: the prayer would profit them also, since it concerned them that he should not be killed in Judea, and it would be to their advantage that he come cheerful and free from grief, to labour among them the more strenuously; the refreshing, he notes, was mutual. Calvin closes on the title given God in the blessing that follows. Paul often speaks of him as the God of peace, especially when referring to discords among Christians, which intimates that there were strifes among these; and from the universal word Calvin concludes that he prayed not simply that God would favour the Romans in general, but that he would rule and guide every one of them, and keep them united.

Clarke adds that they thought they should do God service by destroying him, not only as an apostate from the Jewish religion but as one labouring to subvert it. Wesley explains the urgency: he presses so hard from a sense of the importance of his life to the church, since otherwise he would have rejoiced to depart and be with Christ.

Barnes sets out why they hated him particularly: they could not forget that he had once borne letters of commission from them to persecute the Christians at Damascus, they held him an apostate, and they had been told that he taught all the Jews among the Gentiles to forsake the laws of Moses; his fears, as the result showed, were well founded. On the second petition he finds two grounds of doubt. Many even among Christians might have their minds filled with prejudice from the reports in circulation that he opposed the customs of Moses; and many converts from Judaism might be indisposed to receive an offering made by Gentiles, retaining the old feeling that they were polluted. He fastens on the clause that qualifies the whole request: after all his desires and all their prayers it still depended on the will of God, to which the apostle was desirous to submit. Ellicott judges the prayer partly granted: he escaped with his life from his unbelieving countrymen, but only to be delivered over to the Romans.
